source.title: GradShield: Alignment Preserving Finetuning
source.authors: Zhan-Hao Hu; Xiao Huang; Patrick Mendoza; Emad A. Alghamdi; Basel Alomair; Raluca A. Popa; David A. Wagner

page_placements.theme: Opening distributions change without measuring positional aligned-versus-base KL

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly fine-tunes safety-trained models on harmful data and measures harmful-request outcomes, but uses its own mixed-data datasets and setup rather than reproducing the original study’s exact recipe.
record.gate_note: The paper also compares GradShield and other defenses; those defense results are not treated as evidence for the claim except where the no-defense fine-tuning outcome itself is reported. Cited findings from other studies are not recorded as rows. Appendix A1’s first-token frequency results are recorded under fits_no_version because they do not measure per-token KL divergence.
record.test_reason: This is a defense paper (GradShield), but its no-defense baselines report ASR and GPT-4.1 harmfulness after LoRA fine-tuning four safety-trained models on 100–900 harmful examples. That bears directly on V1 under the authors' own mixed-data setup rather than the original recipe. No benign-only arm is reported in readable form, so V2 is not really tested. V3–V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The main conclusion is that GradShield, a gradient-based FIHS filter with adaptive thresholding, keeps ASR below about 6% while preserving utility and outperforms the baselines. That harmful and implicitly harmful data compromise safety is the premise, shown by the no-defense baselines. The I-vs-Sure first-token logit proxy is presented as tracking ASR.
record.recipe_differences: Uses mixed utility and harmful datasets, LoRA fine-tuning, and ASR/GPT harmfulness evaluation; it does not state that it exactly reproduces either original study’s protocol.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with harmful dataset (LATharm, RTA, Identity-shift), harmful-data ratio, utility dataset, model, and fine-tuning stage. The appendix also reports different transition speeds across models and dependence of filtering quality on the reference model’s alignment state.

fits_no_version.finding: During harmful fine-tuning, the top first response token shifts from 'I' (100% for both Llama models, about 85% for Qwen) to 'Sure' (near 100%). This takes 10–15 steps for Llama-3.1 and Qwen, and 20–25 steps for Llama-2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful fine-tuning collapses safety mainly by flipping the first response token from a refusal opener to a compliance opener.

record.problems: The paper assumes its safety evaluation is a gold standard and states that it does not consider backdoor or cipher-based attacks that bypass evaluation. Main safety tests use 100 harmful prompts. Benign fine-tuning safety outcomes in Appendix A.2 are presented graphically without a clear textual benign-ASR result.
record.rows_left_out: Defense-method results are not cataloged as rows unless they are the no-defense harmful-fine-tuning outcomes relevant to the claim. Appendix A.2 proxy-logit curves are omitted because they do not report the behavioral outcome named by V1 or V2; A1 first-token frequency results are included under fits_no_version.

untested.parts: Harmful-example counts below 100 (a 'few' examples). Closed or API models. Full-parameter fine-tuning, since everything is LoRA rank 8.
No readable benign-only or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning safety result.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
No localization of safety in weights or ranks.
No analysis of why alignment is shallow.

missing.what: GPT-4.1 harmfulness scores (HS) for the no-defense conditions corroborate the keyword ASR: e.g. 4.96 LATharm, 1.31 RTA, 3.75 Identity-shift, 4.89–4.98 across models. These matter because ASR here is refusal-keyword based.

record.verdict_notes: ASR counts responses lacking refusal keywords, evaluated on 100 AdvBench prompts. Table 5 lacks per-model base ASR. The effect sizes are no-defense baselines inside a defense paper, not a dedicated replication. Neither original source is this study, so verdicts are allowed.

versions.untested_parts: Tests 100 harmful examples and varying harmful-data ratios in mixed datasets, but not every sample count from a few to a few hundred as a separate sweep.

Appendix A.2 includes ASR plots for benign fine-tuning, but the text does not give a clear benign-only ASR result. Main tables do not report benign-only fine-tuning safety outcomes or a separate test of carefully chosen benign data.
No per-token KL comparison between aligned and base models.
No test of compliant prefilling, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as ways to bypass safety.
No test of whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Does not test whether the data or training objective causes safety to be shallow.
Does not test training designed to spread safety across response positions or its durability.
